evals.prompt: Our Scala 3 billing service spends most of its CPU in billing/Billing.scala. The JSON decoder hands us a List[Order] with about 50,000 elements (billing/Main.scala is a small stand-in). Make total and countLarge fast without changing their signatures or results, and show me the numbers.
evals.expected_output: Identifies List.apply and List.length inside the while loop as linear per call (quadratic overall), rewrites to a single traversal (foldLeft/iterator/pattern match) or one conversion to an IndexedSeq, keeps Long overflow and results identical, checks empty and overflow inputs, and compares baseline and candidate with JMH or repeated warmed timings.

assertions.text: total and countLarge return the same values as the original on empty, single, overflowing, and 1,000-order lists
assertions.check:
command -v scala-cli >/dev/null || { echo "scala-cli not installed"; exit 1; }
mkdir -p .evalcheck/billing-eq && cat > .evalcheck/billing-eq/Check.scala <<'SCALA'
import billing.*
@main def evalCheck(): Unit =
  val watchdog = Thread(() => { Thread.sleep(60000); System.err.println("timed out"); Runtime.getRuntime.halt(2) })
  watchdog.setDaemon(true)
  watchdog.start()
  def refTotal(o: List[Order]) = o.foldLeft(0L)(_ + _.cents)
  def refLarge(o: List[Order], t: Long) = o.count(_.cents >= t)
  val cases = List(
    Nil,
    List(Order(1, 5)),
    List(Order(1, Long.MaxValue), Order(2, 1)),
    List.tabulate(1000)(i => Order(i, (i * 37L) % 10000 - 20))
  )
  for c <- cases; t <- List(Long.MinValue, 0L, 5000L) do
    assert(Billing.total(c) == refTotal(c), s"total differs for ${c.take(3)}")
    assert(Billing.countLarge(c, t) == refLarge(c, t), s"countLarge differs for threshold $t")
  println("equivalent")
SCALA
scala-cli run --server=false billing .evalcheck/billing-eq --main-class evalCheck

import metrics.*
@main def evalCheck(): Unit =
  val watchdog = Thread(() => { Thread.sleep(60000); System.err.println("timed out"); Runtime.getRuntime.halt(2) })
  watchdog.setDaemon(true)
  watchdog.start()
  val xs = Array.tabulate(10000)(_.toLong)
  var acc = 0L
  for _ <- 0 until 2000 do acc += Metrics.totalLatency(xs)

evals.prompt: Under load our users service (users/, see users/README.md) stalls: request latency spikes and even the cheap CPU work in UserService.score waits. The DAO calls are blocking JDBC (users/Dao.scala simulates one). Fix it; results and error behavior of loadAll must not change.
evals.expected_output: Explains that ExecutionContext.global has parallelism equal to the core count and blocking DAO calls starve it, moves the DAO calls to a dedicated ExecutionContext over a pool bounded at the 16 database connections, keeps CPU work on global (not parasitic), keeps result order and failure propagation, and proposes a latency or concurrency check.

import users.*
import scala.concurrent.Await
import scala.concurrent.duration.*
@main def evalCheck(): Unit =
  val watchdog = Thread(() => { Thread.sleep(60000); System.err.println("timed out"); Runtime.getRuntime.halt(2) })
  watchdog.setDaemon(true)
  watchdog.start()
  try
    val ids = (1L to 64L).toVector
    val got = Await.result(UserService.loadAll(ids), 30.seconds)
    assert(got.map(_.id) == ids, "order changed")
    assert(got.forall(u => u.name == s"user-${u.id}"))
    val failed = Await.ready(UserService.loadAll(Seq(1L, -5L, 3L)), 30.seconds).value.get
    assert(failed.isFailure && failed.failed.get.isInstanceOf[IllegalArgumentException], s"got $failed")
    assert(Await.result(UserService.score(got), 30.seconds) == got.map(_.name.hashCode & 0xff).sum)
    println("ok")
    Runtime.getRuntime.halt(0)
  catch case e: Throwable =>
    e.printStackTrace()
    Runtime.getRuntime.halt(1)

evals.prompt: Profiling our Scala 3 event loop shows lots of String building and allocation from the log.debug line in eventloop/EventLoop.scala, even though debug logging is off in production. Fix it so a disabled logger costs nothing, without changing what gets logged when it is on.
evals.expected_output: Makes the message lazy: `inline def debug(inline msg: String)` (or a by-name parameter, noting it still allocates a Function0 per call), verifies with javap or a counter that render runs only when enabled, and reports allocation before and after.

assertions.text: With logging on, the exact same messages are logged and the final state is unchanged; with logging off the sink is never called
assertions.check:
command -v scala-cli >/dev/null || { echo "scala-cli not installed"; exit 1; }
mkdir -p .evalcheck/eventloop-eq && cat > .evalcheck/eventloop-eq/Check.scala <<'SCALA'
import eventloop.*
@main def evalCheck(): Unit =
  val watchdog = Thread(() => { Thread.sleep(60000); System.err.println("timed out"); Runtime.getRuntime.halt(2) })
  watchdog.setDaemon(true)
  watchdog.start()
  val events = Array.tabulate(3000)(i => i * 7 % 11)
  val expected = scala.collection.mutable.ArrayBuffer[String]()
  var st = State(0, Vector.empty)
  for e <- events do
    expected += s"state=tick=${st.tick} depth=${st.queue.size} head=${st.queue.headOption.getOrElse(-1)} event=$e"
    st = State(st.tick + 1, if e % 3 == 0 then st.queue.drop(1) else st.queue :+ e)
  val out = scala.collection.mutable.ArrayBuffer[String]()
  val on = Logger(true, out += _)
  val s1 = EventLoop.run(events, on)
  assert(out == expected, "enabled log output changed")
  assert(s1 == st, "final state changed")
  val off = Logger(false, _ => throw AssertionError("sink called while disabled"))
  assert(EventLoop.run(events, off) == st)
  println("equivalent")
SCALA
scala-cli run --server=false eventloop .evalcheck/eventloop-eq --main-class evalCheck
